reference.source: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
clinicalPearls: A fracture of the neck of the fifth metacarpal, usually caused by striking a hard object with a clenched fist
There is characteristic apex-dorsal angulation with volar tilt of the metacarpal head; considerable angulation is tolerated here because of the mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint
Rotational malalignment, detected as scissoring or overlap of the fingers on flexion, is not tolerated and must be assessed and corrected
Always inspect for an overlying wound suggesting a fight bite (tooth injury), which carries a serious risk of joint infection
Most fractures are managed conservatively with buddy strapping or an ulnar gutter splint and early mobilisation
Markedly angulated, rotated or multiple fractures may require closed reduction and immobilisation or fixation
Pseudoclawing on attempted extension indicates significant angulation requiring correction
reference.pathophysiology: An axial force transmitted along the fifth metacarpal during a punch concentrates stress at the metaphyseal neck. The thin dorsal cortex fails in tension while the volar cortex is compressed, producing apex-dorsal angulation, and the pull of the intrinsic muscles further flexes the distal fragment volarly. The generous mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint compensates for residual angulation in the sagittal plane, so functional loss is usually minor unless there is malrotation, which foreshortens and crosses the affected finger over its neighbours during flexion.
additionalDifferentials: Carpometacarpal fracture-dislocation of the little finger
Fight-bite injury with metacarpophalangeal joint involvement
additionalInvestigations: Anteroposterior, lateral and oblique hand radiographs
Measurement of the degree of neck angulation on the lateral view
Clinical assessment of rotational alignment via the finger cascade during flexion
Careful wound inspection for a fight-bite breach of the metacarpophalangeal joint
CT reserved for suspected intra-articular extension
redFlags: Rotational deformity with scissoring of the fingers
An open wound over the metacarpophalangeal joint (fight bite) with infection risk
Excessive angulation causing pseudoclawing or functional deficit
Signs of established joint or hand infection
reference.prognosis: Most fractures heal well with good function even with moderate residual angulation because of the mobility of the fifth carpometacarpal joint; rotational malunion and an untreated fight-bite infection are the principal causes of a poor outcome.
pitfalls: Missing malrotation because the sagittal angulation appears acceptable
Overlooking a fight-bite wound and subsequent joint sepsis
Over-treating minor angulation that would remodel or be well tolerated
Failing to check active flexion for finger scissoring
references: Rockwood and Green's Fractures in Adults
